beats.headline: A CITY UNDER THE ICE?
beats.short_title: The Secret Nuclear Base Under Greenland's Ice 🧊 Case #15
beats.comment: Would you live under the ice? 🧊 yes / 🥶 no way
beats.bonus: Camp Century, dug into the Greenland ice sheet in 1959 and powered by a portable nuclear reactor, was the public face of Project Iceworm: a secret US Army plan for 4,000 km of ice tunnels holding up to 600 nuclear missiles. The moving ice made it unworkable, and the camp was abandoned in the 1960s. Its waste is still under the ice.
beats.caption: The US hid a nuclear missile plan inside the Greenland ice.
sources: Wikipedia, Project Iceworm: top-secret US Army plan for 4,000 km of tunnels under the Greenland ice sheet holding up to 600 nuclear missiles; Camp Century (1959) was the public cover; ice movement made it unworkable; cancelled, camp abandoned 1966-67; its waste (incl. diesel, PCBs, radioactive waste) was left under the ice and could re-emerge as the ice melts; details secret until Danish documents released in 1997 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Iceworm (checked 2026-10-26)
Colgan et al., 'The abandoned ice sheet base at Camp Century, Greenland, in a warming climate', Geophysical Research Letters, 2016

The newspapers loved it. But they only got half the story.
See, in 1959, the Army built Camp Century in Greenland.
Tunnels cut into the ice. Bunks, a lab, even a chapel.
And a portable nuclear reactor to keep the lights on.

beats.say: Guess one: an Arctic science lab. That was the cover.
Guess two: a hideout for aliens. No aliens. Just cold.
I licked the wall. Now I'm stuck to it.
Wait. Here's the thing. Greenland is close to the Soviet Union.
Verdict: real. Project Iceworm planned six hundred nuclear missiles under the ice.
Four thousand kilometers of tunnels, moved around so nobody could target them.
Then the ice did something nobody planned for. It moved.
The tunnels squeezed shut. The plan died. The camp was abandoned.
Most of the details stayed secret until 1997.
And the waste they left behind is still down there, waiting for the ice to melt.
A farmer swung the axe at a rooster, and the rooster walked away.
beats.headline: NO HEAD?
beats.short_title: Mike the Headless Chicken Was REAL 🐓 Case #16 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Would you pay to see him? 🐓 yes / 🙈 no
beats.bonus: On 10 September 1945 in Fruita, Colorado, farmer Lloyd Olsen's axe missed the jugular and left one ear and most of the brain stem, so Mike the rooster lived another 18 months. Olsen fed him with an eyedropper and toured him at sideshows. Fruita still holds Mike the Headless Chicken Day every May.
beats.caption: Mike the rooster lived 18 months without most of his head.
sources: Wikipedia, Mike the Headless Chicken: Wyandotte rooster, Fruita, Colorado; beheaded 10 Sep 1945 by Lloyd Olsen; axe missed the jugular, left one ear and most of the brain stem; lived 18 months, fed by eyedropper; died March 1947; Mike the Headless Chicken Day held each May since 1999 — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_the_Headless_Chicken (checked 2026-10-26)
City of Fruita, 'Mike the Headless Chicken Festival' — https://www.fruita.org

Britain designed an aircraft carrier out of ice, and Churchill loved it.
beats.headline: A SHIP OF ICE?
beats.short_title: Britain Planned an Aircraft Carrier Made of ICE 🧊 Case #17
beats.comment: Would you sail on an ice ship? 🧊 yes / 🥶 nope
beats.bonus: Project Habakkuk: in WWII Geoffrey Pyke proposed an unsinkable aircraft carrier made of pykrete, frozen water mixed with wood pulp, which is tougher and slower-melting than plain ice. Churchill and Mountbatten backed it, and a 1,000-ton prototype was built on Patricia Lake in Canada in 1944 before the project was shelved.
beats.caption: Britain really tried to build an aircraft carrier out of ice.
sources: Wikipedia, Project Habakkuk: WWII British plan (Geoffrey Pyke) for an aircraft carrier made of pykrete, ice mixed with wood pulp; backed by Mountbatten and Churchill; a 1,000-ton prototype was built on Patricia Lake, Alberta, in 1944; shelved as costs rose; the final design displaced 2.2 million tons; at the 1943 Quebec Conference a bullet fired at a pykrete block ricocheted, grazing Admiral Ernest King's trouser leg (accounts differ) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Habakkuk (checked 2026-10-26)
Parks Canada, Jasper National Park: Habakkuk prototype remains in Patricia Lake

beats.say: Why shoot the ice? Guess.
Subscribe. New case every day.
It was the strangest weapons test of the war. But it made sense.
See, in 1942, German submarines were sinking ships in the Atlantic.
Planes couldn't reach the middle of the ocean. Not enough fuel.
So an inventor named Geoffrey Pyke had an idea. A floating airfield. Made of ice.
Guess one: plain ice. No. It cracks and melts.
Guess two: a giant iceberg with a runway. Too slow, and it melts too.
I tried skating on it. Sauce everywhere.
Wait. Here's the trick. Mix the ice with sawdust.
Verdict: true. Ice plus wood pulp was tough enough to stop a bullet. They called it pykrete.
Churchill loved it. Mountbatten pushed it.
They built a test ship on a lake in Canada. A thousand tons.
The real ship would have weighed two million tons.
Then the costs exploded, planes got better range, and it was shelved.
At one meeting, the test bullet reportedly bounced off and grazed an American admiral's trousers.
Soviet scientists drilled seven miles into the Earth, and a story said they heard screams.

shots.photo: Soviet stamp of the Kola Superdeep Borehole (1987)

beats.headline: SCREAMS FROM HELL?
beats.short_title: The 'Well to Hell': Did Scientists Hear Screams? 🔥 Case #18
beats.comment: Would you listen down the hole? 👂 yes / 🙉 no way
beats.bonus: The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia reached 12,262 metres (about 7.6 miles) in 1989, the deepest hole ever drilled. Drilling stopped when rock temperatures hit about 180 °C, and the hole is now welded shut under a rusty metal cap. The 'screams from hell' story has no scientific record behind it.
beats.caption: The deepest hole on Earth and the 'Well to Hell' legend.
sources: Wikipedia, Kola Superdeep Borehole: SG-3 reached 12,262 m (40,230 ft) in 1989; drilling stopped at about 180 °C; drilling ended 1995; the borehole is welded shut — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Superdeep_Borehole (checked 2026-10-26)
Snopes, 'Well to Hell' (the screams story traced to 1989-90 broadcasts and newsletters, with no source in the project's records) — https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/well-to-hell/

The CIA's director ordered the files destroyed, and twenty thousand pages survived anyway.
beats.headline: MIND CONTROL?
beats.short_title: MKUltra: The CIA Mind-Control Program Was REAL 🔍 Case #19
beats.comment: Did you know this was real? ✅ yes / 😳 no idea
beats.bonus: MKUltra was a CIA program (1953 to the early 1970s) that tested drugs and other methods on people, some of them unwitting. Director Richard Helms ordered its files destroyed in 1973, but about 20,000 documents survived because they were misfiled with financial records, and a 1977 FOIA request found them.
beats.caption: The CIA really ran a mind-control research program, and the proof survived by accident.
sources: Wikipedia, MKUltra: CIA program begun 1953 on the order of Allen Dulles and led by Sidney Gottlieb, terminated 1972-73; used unwitting US and Canadian subjects; revealed by the Church Committee and Rockefeller Commission in 1975; Helms ordered the files destroyed in 1973; about 20,000 documents survived because they were misfiled in a financial records building and were found through a 1977 FOIA request, leading to Senate hearings — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MKUltra (checked 2026-10-26)
US Senate, 'Project MKULTRA, the CIA's Program of Research in Behavioral Modification', joint hearing, 3 August 1977

Three schoolgirls started laughing, and they couldn't stop.
beats.headline: A LAUGHING PLAGUE?
beats.short_title: The 1962 Laughter Epidemic Was REAL 😂 Case #20 Meatball Investigates
beats.comment: Could this happen today? 😬 yes / 🙅 no way
beats.bonus: The Tanganyika laughter epidemic began on 30 January 1962 at a girls' boarding school in Kashasha, near Lake Victoria in what is now Tanzania. It started with three girls, spread to about 1,000 people and closed 14 schools before dying out about 18 months later. Researchers class it as mass psychogenic illness (mass hysteria), not an infection.
beats.caption: In 1962 a laughing outbreak closed 14 schools.
sources: Wikipedia, Tanganyika laughter epidemic: began 30 Jan 1962 at a mission boarding school for girls in Kashasha; started with three girls, 95 of 159 pupils affected; about 1,000 people affected and 14 schools shut; symptoms lasted hours to 16 days; ended about 18 months after it began; classed as mass hysteria — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_laughter_epidemic (checked 2026-10-26)
Hempelmann, C. F., 'The laughter of the 1962 Tanganyika laughter epidemic', Humor 20(1), 2007

Verdict: real. Mass panic, not a germ.
The cure was the hardest part. Closing the schools.
Soldiers drove out with machine guns to fight an army of birds.
beats.headline: SOLDIERS VS BIRDS?
beats.short_title: The Great Emu War of 1932 Was REAL 🪖 Case #21 Meatball Investigates
beats.bonus: In late 1932 the Australian Army sent soldiers with two Lewis machine guns to cull about 20,000 emus eating Western Australian wheat. The birds split into small groups, a gun jammed, and the operation was withdrawn. Defence Minister Sir George Pearce was later mocked in parliament as the 'Minister of the Emu War'.
beats.caption: Australia really sent soldiers with machine guns against emus.
sources: Wikipedia, Emu War: Nov-Dec 1932, Western Australia; about 20,000 emus raiding wheat farms; soldiers under Major G.P.W. Meredith with two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds; the birds split into small groups; a gun jammed after 12 birds; 986 confirmed kills; the operation was withdrawn; Defence Minister Sir George Pearce was later called 'Minister of the Emu War' in parliament — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emu_War (checked 2026-10-26)
Murray Johnson, '"Feathered foes": soldier settlers and Western Australia's "Emu War" of 1932', Journal of Australian Studies, 2006

It should have been easy. But the birds had a plan.
See, in 1932, about twenty thousand emus invaded the wheat farms of Western Australia.
Many farmers were ex-soldiers. They asked for machine guns.
The army sent two Lewis guns and ten thousand bullets.
Guess one: the army won in a day. Nope.
Guess two: the emus flew away. Emus can't fly.
I got in the truck. An emu outran it.
Wait. Here's the thing about emus. They split up and ran.
Verdict: true. The army fought the emus, and the emus mostly won.
At the dam, the gun jammed after twelve birds. The rest scattered.
Small groups, too fast, too spread out to hit.
An emu can sprint about fifty kilometers an hour. The trucks couldn't keep up.
Within weeks, the army withdrew. The emus stayed.
Back in parliament, the defence minister was mocked as the Minister of the Emu War.
